claim: Cited (with varadi2022) for 'The completion of the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database'; bib check; confirm it is the AlphaFold method paper.
verdict: VERIFIED (as the AlphaFold method paper; it does not describe the database)
quote: Here we provide the first computational method that can regularly predict protein structures with atomic accuracy even in cases in which no similar structure is known. We validated an entirely redesigned version of our neural network-based model, AlphaFold, in the challenging 14th Critical Assessment of protein Structure Prediction (CASP14)15, demonstrating accuracy competitive with experimental structures in a majority of cases and greatly outperforming other methods.
grep: Here we provide the first computational method that can regularly predict protein structures
bib_notes: Crossref 10.1038/s41586-021-03819-2: Nature 596(7873):583-589, print 2021-08-26 (online 2021-07-15), 34 authors, first author John Jumper. Bib entry matches (issue 7873 omitted, fine).
notes: The paper never mentions the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database; the only database-scale statement is 'in a companion paper39, we demonstrate the application of AlphaFold to the entire human proteome39.' (grep 'companion paper'). Citing it for the 'completion' of the DB is loose; varadi2024 is the paper that documents the 214M-structure database.

claim: Cited for 'The completion of the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database ... With predicted structures for over 200 million proteins spanning virtually all known organisms'.
verdict: NOT SUPPORTED (this paper reports >360,000 structures across 21 proteomes, not >200 million)
quote: The initial release of AlphaFold DB contains over 360,000 predicted structures across 21 model-organism proteomes, which will soon be expanded to cover most of the (over 100 million) representative sequences from the UniRef90 data set.
grep: contains over 360,000 predicted structures across 21 model-organism proteomes
bib_notes: Crossref 10.1093/nar/gkab1061: Nucleic Acids Research 50(D1):D439-D444, print 2022-01-07 (online 2021-11-17), 27 authors, first author Mihaly Varadi. Bib entry matches.
notes: Also: 'This will be followed by another update in 2022 to include structures for most representative sequences from the UniRef90 data set (>100 million structures).' (grep '>100 million structures'). Neither the 200M+ figure nor 'virtually all known organisms' appears in this paper; the >214M figure is stated in varadi2024. Suggest citing varadi2024 at line 101.

claim: 'The AlphaFold Protein Structure Database provides predicted structures for 214 million proteins across UniProt'; line 450 'the full AlphaFold universe'.
verdict: VERIFIED (214 million; UniProtKB sequences with listed exclusions; organism coverage not quantified beyond 48 proteome TAR files)
quote: The database provides access to over 214 million predicted structures, although some sequences might be outdated compared to UniProt due to less frequent data releases in the AlphaFold DB.
grep: The database provides access to over 214 million predicted structures
bib_notes: Crossref 10.1093/nar/gkad1011: NAR 52(D1):D368-D375, print 2024-01-05 (online 2023-11-02), 23 authors, first author Mihaly Varadi. TITLE IS TRUNCATED in the bib: full title is 'AlphaFold Protein Structure Database in 2024: providing structure coverage for over 214 million protein sequences'. Volume/issue/pages/year correct.
notes: UniProt coverage statement: 'the MMseqs2 tool first clustered 214 million UniProtKB protein sequences from AlphaFold DB' (grep '214 million UniProtKB protein sequences'). Exclusions: 'The following sequences are not covered in the database: (i) those that are less than 16 amino acids, or (ii) >2700 for SwissProt or proteome sequences and 1280 for other UniProt sequences, or (iii) those that contain non-standard amino acids, or (iv) are not in the UniProt ‘one sequence per gene’ FASTA file, or (v) viral proteins.' The paper does not say 'virtually all known organisms'; it says 'the EMBL-EBI’s FTP area hosts TAR files for proteomes of 48 organisms'. Abstract: 'amassing over 214 million predicted protein structures' (grep 'amassing over 214 million').

(grep 'family membership and GO terms'). Relevant to line 472: 'UniProt releases are published every eight weeks.' (grep 'every eight weeks'). The paper is an acceptable generic citation for UniProtKB, but it is not evidence for Pfam cross-references.

The GO paper also says UniProt-GOA electronic annotations dominate: 'For most organisms, all annotations are electronic annotations generated via various pipelines' (grep 'all annotations are electronic annotations').

claim: 'electronically propagated GO annotations may create artificial co-occurrence'.
verdict: UNVERIFIABLE (abstract + Key Points only; retrieved text mentions neither electronic/IEA annotations nor co-occurrence)
quote: Functional profiling using GO annotations is often performed in an incorrect or inappropriate way. Important issues related to this include a tendency to perform only enrichment testing, using an incorrect reference set, lack of or an inappropriate correction for multiple comparisons, indiscriminate propagation of annotations through the hierarchy, and ignoring the correlations between GO terms.
grep: indiscriminate propagation of annotations through the hierarchy
bib_notes: Crossref 10.1038/nrg2363: Nature Reviews Genetics 9(7):509-515, print July 2008 (online 2008-05-13); authors Seung Yon Rhee, Valerie Wood, Kara Dolinski, Sorin Draghici. Bib entry matches.
notes: Retrieved: PubMed abstract (PMID 18475267) and the nature.com page (abstract + 5 'Key Points'; full text paywalled, no OA copy found). Closest retrieved statements: 'Evidence codes, annotations for unknown functions and annotation qualifiers are vital aspects of GO annotations, but these crucial features of GO annotation are often overlooked.' (grep 'Evidence codes, annotations for unknown functions') and the quoted key point on propagation through the hierarchy and correlations between GO terms. 'Artificial co-occurrence' created by electronic propagation is therefore an INFERENCE by the manuscript, not a statement found in the retrieved text; whether the full text discusses IEA bias could not be checked.

claim: One-sided empirical permutation p-value with the +1 correction; resolution 1/101 with 100 permutations (lines 364, 385).
verdict: VERIFIED (estimator (b+1)/(m+1) is the paper's valid permutation p-value)
quote: In effect, the randomization test replaces the unknown tail probability p∞ with a biased estimator (b + 1)/(m + 1), the amount of positive bias being just enough to allow for the uncertainty of estimation and to produce a test with the correct size.
grep: replaces the unknown tail probability p∞ with a biased estimator (b + 1)/(m + 1)
bib_notes: Crossref 10.2202/1544-6115.1585: Statistical Applications in Genetics and Molecular Biology vol 9 issue 1, online 2010-10-31; PubMed: 'Stat Appl Genet Mol Biol. 2010;9:Article39'. Bib '9(1):39, 2010' is consistent (Article 39). arXiv 1603.05766v1 states 'Published 31 October 2010; corrected 9 February 2011'.
notes: Also: 'The valid but conservative p-value pu has been recommended by a number of authors including Davison and Hinkley (1997), Manly (1997) and Ernst (2004).' (grep 'valid but conservative p-value pu') and 'there is no justification for using an invalid p-value when a valid p-value, in the form of pu , is readily available for no extra cost.' Resolution: 'P( p̂ ≤ α) is never less than 1/(m + 1)' (grep 'never less than 1/(m + 1)'); with m=100, b=0 gives 1/101 as the tex states. The paper's third recommendation is the exact p-value pe (statmod::permp), which is slightly smaller than pu.
